title: Fewest Replacements for a Gapless Run
statement:
You get an array nums of length n. In one move you may overwrite any element with any integer you like.

The array is gapless when its values are all different and max − min = n − 1. In other words, the values are exactly n consecutive integers, in any order.

Return the smallest number of moves that makes nums gapless.

examples.why: The values are 2, 3, 4, 5 in some order. Nothing to change.
Keep 6, 7 and 9, which all fit in the run 6..10. The 1 and the second 6 must be rewritten (to 8 and 10). A repeated value can never be kept twice.
A run of 4 values starting at 1 is 1..4, not 1..5. It holds 1, 2, 3, so only the 5 changes.

hints: You never have to touch the values you keep. So flip the question: what is the largest number of values you can keep?
The kept values must be distinct and fit inside one window [s, s + n − 1]. Duplicates are useless, so work on the sorted distinct values.
Slide over the sorted distinct values. For each left end s, move a right pointer while values stay ≤ s + n − 1. The count inside is what you keep; the answer is n minus the best count.

explain.intuition:
Every move rewrites one value, and a value you keep stays as it is. So the answer is n minus the most values you can leave alone. Values you keep must be distinct and must all lie in one window of n consecutive integers, because that is what the final array looks like.

The best window can always start at a value you keep: slide it right until its left edge hits the smallest kept value and nothing is lost. So sort the distinct values and, for each one as the left edge s, count how many distinct values fall in [s, s + n − 1]. As s grows the right edge only moves right, which is a classic sliding window.
steps: Remove duplicates and sort: u holds the distinct values in increasing order.
For each i, advance j while j < u.length and u[j] ≤ u[i] + n − 1.
The window u[i..j−1] can all be kept: update best = max(best, j − i).
Return n − best, where n is the original length, duplicates included.
pitfalls: Using the number of distinct values as the window width. The final run must have n values, the full original length.
Off by one on the window: values from s to s + n − 1, not s + n. In [1, 2, 3, 5] the wrong edge would keep all four.
Keeping duplicates. Two equal values can never both stay, so count distinct values only.

solutions.title: Try every left edge, count by scanning
solutions.idea: For each distinct value as the start of the run, scan all distinct values and count those inside the window.

solutions.title: Sorted distinct values + sliding window
solutions.idea: As the left edge moves right, the right edge never moves back, so one pass with two pointers counts every window.

followups: Replace the moving right pointer with a binary search for s + n − 1. When would you prefer that version?
Now each move may only change a value by +1 or −1, and you count total steps. How does the problem change?
lcTitle: Minimum Number of Operations to Make Array Continuous
